title: Chemotaxis-induced linear instabilities and pattern formation in a reaction-diffusion model
abstract: We study linear instabilities and pattern formation in a spatially extended Selkov model for glycolysis with diffusion and chemotactic interactions between two species. Linear stability analysis reveals two distinct bifurcations: a zero-wavevector, finite-frequency Hopf bifurcation leading to spatially homogeneous oscillations, and a finite-wavevector Turing instability with a saddle-node bifurcation leading to stationary inhomogeneous patterns. The selected wavevector, $k_c$, depends sensitively on the nature and strength of chemotaxis and varies nonmonotonically with the chemotaxis parameters, allowing re-entrant transitions between homogeneous and patterned states. For sufficiently strong chemotaxis, when the two species mutually attract or mutually repel each other, an unusual instability emerges in which the preferred wavevector diverges as a finite threshold in chemotactic strength is approached. We complement the linear analysis with extensive direct numerical simulations (DNS) of the nonlinear partial differential equations in two dimensions. The DNS confirm the predicted instabilities and their nonmonotonic and re-entrant character, and also reveal spatially uniform oscillatory states for suitable parameters. The stationary patterns include spots and, unexpectedly, stable stripes. We further uncover transitions between spot and stripe morphologies controlled by chemotactic strength and diffusivity ratios. The stability of the striped states is consistent with linear amplitude equations, whereas the spot-stripe transition is attributed to nonlinear effects beyond linear stability. Our results demonstrate that chemotaxis can act as a nonmonotonic control parameter for instability selection, wavelength selection, re-entrant pattern formation, and nonlinear pattern morphology in reaction-diffusion systems.
summary: This paper analyzes pattern formation in a reaction-diffusion system modeling glycolysis that includes chemotaxis. Using linear stability analysis and DNS, the authors demonstrate that chemotaxis profoundly controls the resulting spatial patterns, leading to complex, nonmonotonic transitions between different stable states like spots and stripes. The work highlights chemotaxis as a powerful control parameter for pattern selection in non-equilibrium systems.
main_problem: The study investigates linear instabilities and pattern formation in a reaction-diffusion model that incorporates chemotactic interactions between two species.
main_result: The model exhibits complex pattern selection, showing that chemotaxis acts as a nonmonotonic control parameter capable of inducing re-entrant transitions between homogeneous and patterned states, and controlling the morphology between spots and stripes.
method: The research employs linear stability analysis to determine bifurcation points and selected wavevectors, which are then complemented by extensive two-dimensional Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) of the nonlinear partial differential equations.
model_or_system: The system is a spatially extended Selkov model for glycolysis, modeled by two coupled reaction-diffusion PDEs describing the concentrations of two species ($\phi$ and $\psi$). These equations include standard diffusion terms and nonlinear chemotactic coupling terms.
key_observables: Bifurcation types (Hopf, Turing), selected wavevector ($k_c$), pattern morphologies (spots and stripes), and the dependence of these on chemotaxis strength.
important_parameters: Chemotaxis coefficients ($\xi_1, \xi_2$), diffusion coefficients ($D_1, D_2$), and the wavevector $k$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes periodic boundary conditions and examines the infinite system size limit for linear stability analysis.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate pattern formation (uniform to periodic to stripe-like) as a function of diffusion coefficients and show the variation of pattern amplitudes ($\Delta\phi, \Delta\psi$) across different chemotactic regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically moves from linear stability analysis to identify bifurcations, followed by DNS validation of the predicted instabilities and the investigation of nonlinear pattern transitions (spot-stripe) using amplitude equations.
why_interesting: While focused on chemical kinetics, the mathematical framework of pattern selection, instability analysis, and non-equilibrium dynamics (like those seen in active matter) shares deep theoretical parallels with phase transitions and pattern formation studied in AMO physics and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
